mainTopic: Proofs for תחיית המתים, גביהא בן פסיסא's debates before אלכסנדרוס מוקדון, and the start of אנטונינוס's question about judging body and soul
overview: This amud brings several proofs for תחיית המתים. The קיסר's daughter shows that a craftsman who can form things from water can surely form them from clay, and דבי רבי ישמעאל bring a קל וחומר from broken glass that can be fixed. רבי אמי answers a מין with a parable about a king's palace, then gives examples from nature: a creature that forms out of earth, and snails that fill a mountain overnight after rain. גביהא בן פסיסא answers another מין: if people who never existed come to life, those who once lived surely can. The גמרא then tells of three cases גביהא won before אלכסנדרוס מוקדון, against בני אפריקיא, בני מצרים, and בני ישמעאל with בני קטורה. Each time he uses the תורה, the same source they quoted, to defeat their claim. The amud ends as אנטונינוס argues to רבי that body and soul can each blame the other for sin, and רבי starts a parable about a king's orchard that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The emperor's daughter offers to answer with a parable
steps.stepSummary: The קיסר's daughter tells her father to leave רבן גמליאל alone, because she will answer the challenge. She asks which of two craftsmen is more impressive.
steps.simpleTranslation: His daughter said to him: Leave him, and I will answer him. There are two craftsmen in our city. One forms things from water, and one forms things from clay. Which of them is more praiseworthy?
steps.whatsHappening: The daughter is setting up a parable to answer the challenge against תחיית המתים. She asks her father a question so that his own answer will lead to her point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before this, the קיסר had challenged רבן גמליאל by saying that dust cannot come back to life. The daughter does not argue directly. She builds a comparison and lets her father reach the conclusion himself.

keyTerms.meaning: A craftsman who forms things, such as a potter

phrases.english: His daughter said to him:
phrases.notes: This is the emperor's daughter. Her father had just challenged רבן גמליאל about the dead coming back to life.

phrases.english: Leave him, and I will answer him.
There are two craftsmen in our city:
one forms things from water,
and one forms things from clay.
Which of them is more praiseworthy?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרָה לֵיהּ בְּרַתֵּיה: שִׁבְקֵיהּ, וַאֲנָא מַהְדַּרְנָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the daughter's answer to the קיסר's challenge, which came just before this section.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which craftsman shows more skill: the one who works with water or the one who works with clay?

steps.title: The emperor picks the craftsman who works with water
steps.stepSummary: The קיסר answers that the craftsman who forms things from water is the more impressive one.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to her: The one who forms things from water.
steps.whatsHappening: The קיסר answers his daughter's question. Without realizing it, he gives her exactly what she needs for her argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Forming anything out of water is far harder than forming it out of clay, because water has no shape. By admitting this, the קיסר agrees that the harder job is the greater sign of skill.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהּ: זֶה שֶׁיּוֹצֵר מִן הַמַּיִם.
phrases.english: He said to her: The one who forms things from water.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהּ: זֶה שֶׁיּוֹצֵר מִן הַמַּיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the daughter's question from step 1.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The craftsman who works with water is more impressive.

steps.title: If He can form from water, He can surely form from clay
steps.stepSummary: The daughter concludes with a קל וחומר: someone who can form things from water can certainly form them from clay.
steps.simpleTranslation: She said to him: If he can form from water, can he not all the more so form from clay?
steps.whatsHappening: The daughter finishes her answer to the challenge. If God could create from water, which is the harder material, He can surely bring people back from dust.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed that dust is too poor a material to make a living person. The daughter turns it around. Dust is like clay, the easier material, and God already did the harder job when He first created the world.

keyTerms.meaning: An argument from a harder case to an easier one

steps.whatToRemember: The daughter's point: bringing people back from dust is the easier task compared to what God already did in creating the world.

phrases.english: She said to him: From water he forms,
from clay, all the more so, no?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרָה לוֹ: מִן הַמַּיִם צָר, מִן הַטִּיט לֹא כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the קיסר's answer from step 2 to build the קל וחומר.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Dust cannot become a living person again.
steps.terutzMaskana: God, who created from water, can surely re-form people from dust.

steps.title: A קל וחומר from glass vessels
steps.stepSummary: דבי רבי ישמעאל teach that glass vessels, made by human breath, can be fixed after they break. People, whose souls come from God's breath, can surely be restored.
steps.simpleTranslation: דבי רבי ישמעאל taught: There is a קל וחומר from glass vessels. Glass vessels are made by the breath of a human being, and if they break they can be fixed. A human being, made by the breath of הקדוש ברוך הוא, all the more so.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another proof for תחיית המתים from a ברייתא of דבי רבי ישמעאל. It compares broken glass to a person who has died.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Glass is blown by a person's breath, and broken glass can be melted down and blown again. A person was made through God's breath, which is far greater. So a person who "breaks" by dying can surely be made again.

keyTerms.meaning: The study hall of רבי ישמעאל

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:
There is a kal vachomer from glass vessels:
Just as glass vessels,
which are made by the breath of flesh and blood,
if they break, they can be fixed,

phrases.aramaic: בָּשָׂר וָדָם שֶׁבְּרוּחוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא –
phrases.english: then flesh and blood, made by the breath of the Holy One, Blessed be He,
how much more so!

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּבֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל תָּנָא: קַל וָחוֹמֶר מִכְּלֵי זְכוּכִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, separate proof for תחיית המתים, also built on a קל וחומר.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא of דבי רבי ישמעאל: a קל וחומר from broken glass that can be fixed.

steps.title: A מין asks how dust can come back to life
steps.stepSummary: A מין challenges רבי אמי: You say the dead will live, but they turn into dust, and dust cannot live.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain heretic said to רבי אמי: You say that the dead will live. But they become dust! Does dust come to life?
steps.whatsHappening: A new story begins. A מין raises the same challenge against תחיית המתים, this time to רבי אמי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The attack is based on the physical state of the dead. Once a body has decayed into dust, nothing seems left that could live again.

keyTerms.meaning: A heretic, someone who denies Torah beliefs
Those who lie down, meaning the dead

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הָהוּא מִינָא לְרַבִּי אַמֵּי:
phrases.english: A certain heretic said to Rabbi Ami:
You say that the dead will live.
But they become dust,
and does dust come to life?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הָהוּא מִינָא לְרַבִּי אַמֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story with the same challenge the קיסר raised earlier.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The dead turn into dust, and dust cannot become alive.

steps.title: רבי אמי's parable of the king's palace
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי tells of a king whose servants built him a palace where there was no water or earth. When it fell, they said they could not rebuild it where there was water and earth.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I will give you a parable. What is this like? A human king told his servants: Go build me a great palace in a place with no water or earth. They went and built it. Some time later it fell. He told them: Go back and build it in a place that has earth and water. They said to him: We cannot.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אמי starts his answer with a story. The story is a setup, and its point comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The servants managed the hard job, building with no materials. Then they claim they cannot do the easy job, building with materials. The parable is arranged to show how unreasonable that claim is.

keyTerms.meaning: I will give you a parable

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the servants are reasonable here. The parable is built so that their refusal looks foolish: they already did the harder job.

phrases.english: He said to him: I will give you a parable.
What is this like?
To a flesh-and-blood king who said to his servants:
Go and build me a great palace
in a place where there is no water and earth.
They went and built it.
Some time later, it fell.
He said to them: Go back and build it
in a place where there is earth and water.
They said to him: We are unable.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אֶמְשׁוֹל לְךָ מָשָׁל. לְמָה הַדָּבָר דּוֹמֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins רבי אמי's answer to the מין's challenge from step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A parable is set up in which servants did the hard building job but refuse the easy one.

steps.title: The king's angry קל וחומר
steps.stepSummary: The angry king tells his servants: if you built without water and earth, you can surely build with them.
steps.simpleTranslation: He became angry at them and said to them: In a place with no water and earth you built! Now that there is water and earth, how much more so!
steps.whatsHappening: This is the punchline of רבי אמי's parable and his answer to the מין. God created man from nothing, so He can surely bring him back from dust.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מין thought dust was a problem. רבי אמי shows it is actually an advantage: having material makes the job easier than creating from nothing, which God already did.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי אמי's point: creating from nothing is harder than rebuilding from dust, so תחיית המתים is surely possible for God.

phrases.english: He became angry at them and said to them:
In a place with no water and earth you built,
now that there is water and earth,
how much more so!

steps.triggerLanguage: כָּעַס עֲלֵיהֶם, וְאָמַר לָהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the parable from step 6 and applies it to the challenge.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Dust is too poor a material to bring back a living person.
steps.terutzMaskana: God created man from nothing, so rebuilding him from dust is easier.

steps.title: Proof from the creature that forms out of earth
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי adds a proof from nature: a creature in the valley that is half flesh and half earth one day becomes fully flesh the next.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you do not believe it, go out to the valley and see a creature that today is half flesh and half earth. Tomorrow it develops and becomes all flesh.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אמי backs up his parable with something the מין can see for himself. Living flesh can form out of earth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The parable was a logical argument. Now רבי אמי gives a real-world example showing that earth can turn into a living body, which is exactly what the מין denied.

keyTerms.meaning: A creature, like a mouse, believed to form from earth

phrases.english: And if you do not believe,
go out to the valley and see an akhbar
that today is half flesh and half earth;
tomorrow it develops and becomes all flesh.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם אִי אַתָּה מַאֲמִין, צֵא לַבִּקְעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a proof from nature to support the parable's conclusion.
steps.raayaObject: Living flesh can come from earth.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The עכבר in the valley that turns from half earth into full flesh.

steps.title: Maybe it only happens over a long time?
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי expects a pushback: perhaps such creatures only form slowly, over a long period.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps you will say this takes a long time?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אמי raises a possible objection to his own proof before the מין can, and he will answer it in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone could say the example of the creature only shows slow natural development. That would be different from a sudden revival of the dead. This line sets up the snail proof.

phrases.english: Lest you say: over a long time?

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁמָּא תֹּאמַר לִזְמַן מְרוּבֶּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the strength of the proof in step 8.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Creatures forming from earth might take a long time, unlike the sudden revival claimed for תחיית המתים.

steps.title: The snails that fill the mountain overnight
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי answers that on a mountain with only one snail today, after rain tomorrow it is full of snails.
steps.simpleTranslation: Go up the mountain and see that today there is only one snail on it. Tomorrow rain falls, and it is entirely filled with snails.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אמי answers the objection from step 9. He shows that many living creatures can appear very quickly, in just one day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The snail example removes the "long time" objection. Life can appear suddenly and in great numbers. This supports the idea that God can revive the dead quickly.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי אמי gives two kinds of answers: a parable showing logically that rebuilding from dust is easier, and proofs from nature that life can come quickly from earth.

phrases.english: Go up the mountain and see

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁהַיּוֹם אֵין בּוֹ אֶלָּא חִלָּזוֹן אֶחָד,
phrases.english: that today there is only one snail on it;
tomorrow rain falls
and it is entirely filled with snails.

steps.triggerLanguage: עֲלֵה לָהָר וּרְאֵה שֶׁהַיּוֹם אֵין בּוֹ אֶלָּא חִלָּזוֹן אֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection raised in step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A new example from nature that removes the objection
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Life forming from earth only happens slowly.
steps.terutzMaskana: Life can appear suddenly and in great numbers, as the snails after rain show.

steps.title: A heretic mocks belief in the dead coming back to life
steps.stepSummary: A מין challenges גביהא בן פסיסא: people who are alive end up dying, so how can you claim the dead will live?
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain heretic said to גביהא בן פסיסא: Woe to you, wicked ones, who say the dead will live! Those who live die. How can the dead live?
steps.whatsHappening: A new story starts. A מין attacks the belief in תחיית המתים by pointing to what we see every day: living people die, and nobody comes back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His argument is based on experience. The world only moves from life to death, so going from death back to life seems impossible to him. He even calls the believers 'wicked' for saying it.

keyTerms.meaning: A heretic who denies Jewish beliefs
A clever Jew known for winning debates

phrases.english: A certain heretic said
to Geviha ben Pesisa:
Woe to you, wicked ones,
who say the dead will live!
Those who live die, so how can the dead live?

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר ליה ההוא מינא לגביהא בן פסיסא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new story that continues the theme of defending תחיית המתים, like רבי אמי's proofs in steps 6 to 10.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Experience shows only that the living die. Nobody has seen the dead come back.

steps.title: If those who never lived come to life, surely those who once lived can
steps.stepSummary: גביהא turns the insult around and answers with a קל וחומר: people who never existed are born, so people who already lived can surely live again.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Woe to you, wicked ones, who say the dead will not live! If those who never were alive come to life, those who were alive, all the more so!
steps.whatsHappening: גביהא answers the מין, and uses the same 'woe to you, wicked ones' line back at him. He points out that every birth is a creature coming to life out of nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a קל וחומר. Making life where there was nothing at all is harder than bringing back someone who already existed. Since we see the harder thing happen every day, the easier thing is certainly possible.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it not all the more so? (a קל וחומר)

steps.whatToRemember: גביהא's answer: if life can come from nothing, life can surely come back to what once lived.

phrases.english: He said to him: Woe to you, wicked ones,
who say the dead will not live!
If those who never were alive come to life, then those who once were alive
phrases.notes: He means babies being born: they never existed before, and yet they come to life.

phrases.english: is it not all the more so?

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר ליה ווי לכון חייביא דאמריתון מיתי לא חיין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the מין's challenge in step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: קל וחומר from the creation of new life
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the living die and do not return, coming back to life is impossible.
steps.terutzMaskana: Life is created from nothing all the time, so bringing back those who already lived is even more possible.

steps.title: The angry heretic threatens to kick גביהא
steps.stepSummary: The מין is offended at being called wicked and threatens to kick גביהא and flatten his hump.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: You call me wicked? If I get up, I will kick you and straighten out your crookedness!
steps.whatsHappening: The מין has no answer to the argument, so he gets angry and threatens to hurt גביהא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not a logical point. The story shows the מין losing the argument and turning to insults and violence. It sets up גביהא's witty reply in the next step.

phrases.english: He said to him: You call me wicked?
If I get up, I will kick you
and straighten out your crookedness from you!
phrases.notes: גביהא was a hunchback, so the מין is threatening to flatten his hump.

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר ליה חייביא קרית לי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The מין reacts in anger to the insult in step 12 instead of answering the argument.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The מין answers with a threat instead of an argument.

steps.title: גביהא jokes that the heretic would be a great doctor
steps.stepSummary: גביהא laughs off the threat: if you can straighten my hump, you will be called an expert doctor and earn big fees.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: If you do that, you will be called an expert doctor and collect a large fee.
steps.whatsHappening: גביהא answers the threat with a joke, and the story ends there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He turns the threat into a compliment: straightening a hump would be a medical miracle. It shows how calm and clever he was, which leads into the next story about his debating skill.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִם אַתָּה עוֹשֶׂה כֵּן,
phrases.english: He said to him: If you do that,
you will be called an expert doctor,
and you will collect a large fee.

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר ליה אם אתה עושה כן רופא אומן תקרא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: גביהא's witty reply to the threat in step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Straightening my hump would make you a famous, well-paid doctor.

steps.title: A day of celebration: the usurpers were removed from Judea
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that on the 24th of ניסן the usurpers were removed from יהודה and ירושלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: תנו רבנן: On the twenty-fourth of ניסן the usurpers were removed from יהודה and from ירושלים.
steps.whatsHappening: Since we are talking about גביהא בן פסיסא, the גמרא brings a ברייתא about another debate he won. This line gives the date and the result, and sets up the story that explains it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא first states the happy outcome: the people who had taken over the land were sent away. The next lines explain how it happened.

keyTerms.meaning: Usurpers, people who took land that was not theirs

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
On the twenty-fourth of Nisan
the usurpers were removed
from Judea and from Jerusalem.

steps.triggerLanguage: תנו רבנן בעשרים וארבעה בניסן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story about the same hero, גביהא בן פסיסא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The 24th of ניסן marks the day the usurpers were removed from the land.

steps.title: בני אפריקיא claim the land from a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: בני אפריקיא brought a case before אלכסנדרוס מוקדון, claiming ארץ כנען belongs to them because the תורה calls it the land of כנען and כנען was their ancestor.
steps.simpleTranslation: When בני אפריקיא came to bring a case against ישראל before אלכסנדרוס מוקדון, they said to him: ארץ כנען is ours, as it is written: 'ארץ כנען according to its borders,' and כנען was the father of these people.
steps.whatsHappening: The other side presents its claim. They bring a proof from the תורה itself that the land belongs to them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their reasoning: the תורה names the land after כנען, and they are כנען's descendants, so they are its rightful heirs. This is the claim גביהא will have to answer.

keyTerms.meaning: The people of Afrikiya, who said they came from כנען

phrases.english: When the people of Afrikiya came
to bring a case against Israel
before Alexander of Macedon,

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: אֶרֶץ כְּנַעַן שֶׁלָּנוּ הִיא,
phrases.english: they said to him: The land of Canaan is ours,
as it is written: 'the land of Canaan according to its borders,'
and Canaan was the father of these people.

steps.triggerLanguage: כשבאו בני אפריקיא לדון עם ישראל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the background to the removal of the usurpers mentioned in step 15.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that the land belongs to בני אפריקיא
steps.raayaSupportSource: במדבר 34:2, which calls the land 'ארץ כנען'

steps.title: גביהא asks the חכמים for permission to argue the case
steps.stepSummary: גביהא asks the חכמים to let him argue. If he loses, they can say only a simple person lost. If he wins, they can say the תורה של משה won.
steps.simpleTranslation: גביהא בן פסיסא said to the חכמים: Give me permission and I will go and argue with them before אלכסנדרוס מוקדון. If they beat me, say: You beat a simple person among us. And if I beat them, say to them: The תורה of משה beat you. They gave him permission, and he went and argued with them.
steps.whatsHappening: Before answering the claim, גביהא makes a smart arrangement with the חכמים. This sets up the debate that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His plan means the Jewish people cannot really lose. If he fails, it means nothing, because he is 'just an ordinary person'. If he wins, all the credit goes to the תורה.

keyTerms.meaning: A simple, ordinary person, not a scholar

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ גְּבִיהָא בֶּן פְּסִיסָא לַחֲכָמִים:
phrases.english: Geviha ben Pesisa said to the Sages:
Give me permission and I will go
and argue with them before Alexander of Macedon.
If they beat me, say:
You beat a simple person among us,
and if I beat them,
say to them: The Torah of Moses beat you.

phrases.aramaic: נָתְנוּ לוֹ רְשׁוּת, וְהָלַךְ וְדָן עִמָּהֶם.
phrases.english: They gave him permission, and he went and argued with them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר להו גביהא בן פסיסא לחכמים תנו לי רשות
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the claim of step 16 by arranging who will answer it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: גביהא is given permission to argue for the Jewish people, and nothing is risked if he loses.

steps.title: גביהא asks where their proof comes from
steps.stepSummary: גביהא asks בני אפריקיא for the source of their proof, and they answer: from the תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: From where do you bring proof? They said to him: From the תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: גביהא gets the other side to say that the תורה is their source. This is a setup line for his counter-argument in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once they admit they are relying on the תורה, they have to accept everything the תורה says, including verses that work against them.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶם: מֵהֵיכָן אַתֶּם מְבִיאִים רְאָיָיה?
phrases.english: He said to them: From where do you bring proof?
They said to him: From the Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר להם מהיכן אתם מביאים ראייה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the debate that גביהא was given permission for in step 17.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source of their claim to the land

steps.title: A slave's property belongs to his master
steps.stepSummary: גביהא quotes the curse 'כנען will be a slave of slaves'. Whatever a slave owns belongs to his master, so even if the land was כנען's, it belongs to Israel.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: I too will bring you proof only from the תורה, as it says: 'And he said: Cursed be כנען; a slave of slaves shall he be to his brothers.' A slave who acquired property: whom does the slave belong to, and whom does the property belong to?
steps.whatsHappening: גביהא uses the תורה, the same source they relied on, to defeat their claim.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He does not deny that כנען once owned the land. Instead he shows that it does not matter: כנען was made a slave to his brothers, and a slave and everything he owns belong to the master.
steps.confusionAlert: גביהא does not argue that the land never belonged to כנען. He accepts that it did, and argues that a slave's property goes to his master.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶן: אַף אֲנִי לֹא אָבִיא לָכֶם
phrases.english: He said to them: I too will bring you
proof only from the Torah,
as it says: 'And he said: Cursed be Canaan;
a slave of slaves shall he be to his brothers.'
A slave who acquired property:
whom does the slave belong to, and whom does the property belong to?

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר להן אף אני לא אביא לכם ראייה אלא מן התורה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the תורה, which they accepted as the source in step 18, to answer their claim from step 16.
steps.raayaObject: That the land belongs to Israel and not to בני אפריקיא
steps.raayaSupportSource: בראשית 9:25, together with the rule that a slave's property belongs to his master

steps.title: You also owe us years of service
steps.stepSummary: גביהא adds that בני אפריקיא have not served Israel for many years, so they actually owe more.
steps.simpleTranslation: And not only that, but for many years now you have not served us!
steps.whatsHappening: גביהא pushes his argument one step further. The other side not only loses the land, they also owe Israel for years of unpaid service.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If כנען is Israel's slave, then every year he did not serve is a debt he owes. This turns their claim completely around: they came to collect, and now they owe.

keyTerms.meaning: And not only that, but also

steps.whatToRemember: גביהא beat בני אפריקיא with their own source. The תורה made כנען a slave, so his land belongs to Israel, and he even owes back service.

phrases.english: And not only that, but
for many years now you have not served us!

steps.triggerLanguage: ולא עוד אלא שהרי כמה שנים שלא עבדתונו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the slave argument of step 19 and draws a further claim from it.
steps.raayaObject: That בני אפריקיא owe Israel back service
steps.raayaSupportSource: The slave status of כנען established in step 19

steps.title: בני אפריקיא cannot answer and flee their land
steps.stepSummary: אלכסנדרוס tells בני אפריקיא to answer גביהא. They ask for three days, find no answer, and run away. They leave their sown fields and planted vineyards behind in a שמיטה year.
steps.simpleTranslation: King אלכסנדרוס said to them: Give him an answer! They said to him: Give us three days. He gave them the time. They searched and did not find an answer. Right away they fled, leaving their fields already sown and their vineyards already planted. And that year was the seventh year.
steps.whatsHappening: This ends the case of בני אפריקיא. They have no answer to גביהא, so they give up and run away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They had three full days to think and still could not answer. That shows גביהא's argument from the תורה fully won the case. The note about שביעית adds a bonus: Jews may not plant in a שמיטה year, yet they now had ready-made fields and vineyards.

keyTerms.meaning: Time, a set period to prepare
The seventh year, שמיטה, when fields may not be worked

steps.whatToRemember: The first case ends in total victory. The other side runs away and even leaves behind food for Israel in a שמיטה year.

phrases.english: King Alexander said to them:
Give him a response!

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: תְּנוּ לָנוּ זְמַן שְׁלֹשָׁה יָמִים.
phrases.english: They said to him: Give us time, three days.
He gave them time.
They examined it and did not find a response.
Immediately they fled,
and left their fields while they were sown,
and their vineyards while they were planted.
And that year was the seventh year.

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּדְקוּ וְלֹא מָצְאוּ תְּשׁוּבָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the result of גביהא's argument in steps 19-20: the other side has no answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: בני אפריקיא lose completely. They flee and leave their planted land to Israel in a שמיטה year.

steps.title: Egypt demands back the borrowed silver and gold
steps.stepSummary: A new case: בני מצרים come before אלכסנדרוס מוקדון. They quote the פסוק that the Jews 'borrowed' from Egypt and demand the silver and gold back.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another time, בני מצרים came to bring a case against ישראל before אלכסנדרוס מוקדון. They said to him: It says, 'And ה׳ gave the people favor in the eyes of מצרים, and they lent to them.' Give us back the silver and gold you took from us.
steps.whatsHappening: A brand-new case starts here. Egypt uses a פסוק from the תורה to claim the Jews owe them money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Egypt's proof rests on the word וַיַּשְׁאִלוּם, which means they lent it. A loan must be paid back, so they say the Jews still owe them all that silver and gold.

phrases.aramaic: שׁוּב פַּעַם אַחַת בָּאוּ בְּנֵי מִצְרַיִם
phrases.english: Another time, the people of Egypt came
to bring a case against Israel
before Alexander of Macedon.
They said to him: It says

phrases.aramaic: ״וַה׳ נָתַן אֶת חֵן הָעָם בְּעֵינֵי מִצְרַיִם
phrases.english: "And ה׳ gave the people favor in the eyes of Egypt,
and they lent to them."
phrases.notes: Egypt reads this word as a loan, and a loan has to be paid back.

phrases.english: Give us the silver and gold
that you took from us.

steps.triggerLanguage: שׁוּב פַּעַם אַחַת בָּאוּ בְּנֵי מִצְרַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a second story of the same type as the Afrikiya case.
steps.raayaObject: Egypt's claim that Israel must return the silver and gold
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמות 12:36, the word וַיַּשְׁאִלוּם, meaning 'they lent'

steps.title: גביהא again asks permission to argue
steps.stepSummary: גביהא בן פסיסא again asks the חכמים to let him argue. If he loses, it is only a simple man who lost. If he wins, the תורה של משה won. They agree, and he goes.
steps.simpleTranslation: גביהא בן פסיסא said to the חכמים: Give me permission and I will go argue with them before אלכסנדרוס. If they beat me, tell them: You beat a simple person among us. If I beat them, tell them: The תורה of משה our teacher beat you. They gave him permission, and he went and argued with them.
steps.whatsHappening: This step sets up the next move. גביהא repeats the same plan he used in the first case and goes off to argue.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His plan is safe either way. A loss does not shame the Jewish people, and a win gives the credit to the תורה. The same pattern as step 17 tells us the same kind of victory is coming.

keyTerms.meaning: The Torah of משה our teacher

phrases.english: Geviha ben Pesisa said to the Sages:
Give me permission
and I will go and argue with them before Alexander.
If they defeat me, say to them:
You defeated a simple person among us,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם אֲנִי אֲנַצֵּחַ אוֹתָם, אִמְרוּ לָהֶם:
phrases.english: and if I defeat them, say to them:
The Torah of Moshe our teacher defeated you.
They gave him permission
and he went and argued with them.

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּנוּ לִי רְשׁוּת וְאֵלֵךְ וְאָדוּן עִמָּהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to Egypt's claim in step 22 by sending גביהא to argue.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: גביהא will argue: a loss is only a simple man's loss, and a win is the תורה's win.

steps.title: גביהא asks בני מצרים where their proof comes from
steps.stepSummary: גביהא asks בני מצרים for the source of their proof. They answer: from the תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Where are you bringing your proof from? They said to him: From the תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup step. גביהא makes Egypt admit their proof comes from the תורה, so he can use the תורה against them next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once Egypt agrees the תורה is the source, they must accept everything the תורה says. That includes the parts that work against them. This is the same move as in step 18.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶן: מֵהֵיכָן אַתֶּם מְבִיאִין רְאָיָיה?
phrases.english: He said to them: From where are you bringing proof?
They said to him: From the Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵהֵיכָן אַתֶּם מְבִיאִין רְאָיָיה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: גביהא begins the debate by pinning down Egypt's source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the source of Egypt's proof?

steps.title: Egypt owes wages for 430 years of slave labor
steps.stepSummary: גביהא quotes the פסוק that Israel lived in Egypt for 430 years. He demands wages for the work of 600,000 people whom Egypt enslaved for all those years.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: I too will bring you proof only from the תורה, as it says: 'And the stay of בני ישראל, who lived in מצרים, was four hundred and thirty years.' Give us the wages for the work of 600,000 people whom you enslaved in מצרים for four hundred and thirty years.
steps.whatsHappening: גביהא answers Egypt with a claim of his own from the תורה. Egypt owes Israel wages for hundreds of years of slave work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Egypt said the Jews owe them a loan. גביהא turns it around: Egypt owes payment for the forced work of 600,000 people over 430 years. That debt is far bigger than any silver and gold, so the Jews owe nothing back.

keyTerms.meaning: And the stay, the time they lived

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with the Afrikiya argument. There, גביהא said a slave's things belong to his master. Here he says Egypt owes wages for the slave work it forced on Israel.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶן: אַף אֲנִי לֹא אָבִיא לָכֶם רְאָיָיה
phrases.english: He said to them: I too will not bring you proof
except from the Torah, as it says:
"And the stay of the children of Israel, who lived in Egypt,
was thirty years and four hundred years."
Give us the wages for the work
of 600,000 people
whom you enslaved in Egypt
for four hundred and thirty years.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַף אֲנִי לֹא אָבִיא לָכֶם רְאָיָיה אֶלָּא מִן הַתּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the source Egypt agreed to in step 24 to make a bigger counterclaim.
steps.raayaObject: Israel owes Egypt nothing; Egypt owes Israel far more
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמות 12:40, which says Israel lived in Egypt for 430 years

steps.title: The Egyptians cannot answer and run away
steps.stepSummary: אלכסנדרוס tells בני מצרים to answer גביהא. They ask for three days, find nothing, and flee, leaving their sown fields and planted vineyards in a שמיטה year.
steps.simpleTranslation: אלכסנדרוס מוקדון said to them: Give him an answer! They said: Give us three days. He gave them the time. They searched and found no answer. Right away they left their sown fields and planted vineyards and ran away. And that year was a שמיטה year.
steps.whatsHappening: The Egyptian case ends here. The Egyptians have no reply to גביהא's demand for 430 years of wages, so they give up and run away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: גביהא's counter-claim was far bigger than their claim for the borrowed gold and silver, so they lost completely. The גמרא adds that it was a שמיטה year, a detail that shows how valuable it was to be left fields that were already sown and planted.

keyTerms.meaning: The seventh year, the שמיטה year

steps.whatToRemember: The Egyptian claim fails completely. Their enslavement of Israel outweighs anything Israel took from them.

phrases.english: Alexander of Macedon said to them:
Give him back an answer!

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: תְּנוּ לָנוּ זְמַן שְׁלֹשָׁה יָמִים.
phrases.english: They said to him: Give us time, three days.
He gave them time.
They searched and did not find an answer.
Immediately they left their fields while they were sown,
and their vineyards while they were planted, and fled.
And that year was the seventh year.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהֶן אֲלֶכְּסַנְדְּרוֹס מוֹקְדוֹן: הַחְזִירוּ לוֹ תְּשׁוּבָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the Egyptian case that גביהא's counter-claim in step 25 set up.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: בני מצרים lose the case and flee, and the Jews gain their fields.

steps.title: בני ישמעאל and בני קטורה claim a share of ארץ כנען
steps.stepSummary: A third case: בני ישמעאל and בני קטורה claim ארץ כנען is partly theirs, because the תורה calls both ישמעאל and יצחק sons of אברהם.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another time, the descendants of ישמעאל and of קטורה came to argue with ישראל before אלכסנדרוס. They said: ארץ כנען is ours and yours, because it is written 'These are the generations of ישמעאל son of אברהם,' and it is written 'These are the generations of יצחק son of אברהם.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new case opens. The other children of אברהם bring a proof from the תורה that they deserve part of the land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their argument is about inheritance. Both lines are called "son of אברהם" in the same way, so they claim equal heirs should split the father's land.

keyTerms.meaning: The descendants of קטורה, the wife אברהם married later
To bring a legal case, to argue in judgment

phrases.english: And again, another time, there came
the descendants of Ishmael and the descendants of Keturah
to go to judgment with Israel
before Alexander of Macedon.

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: אֶרֶץ כְּנַעַן שֶׁלָּנוּ וְשֶׁלָּכֶם,
phrases.english: They said to him: The land of Canaan is ours and yours,
as it is written: "And these are the generations of Ishmael, son of Abraham"
and it is written: "These are the generations of Isaac, son of Abraham."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְשׁוּב פַּעַם אַחַת בָּאוּ בְּנֵי יִשְׁמָעֵאל וּבְנֵי קְטוּרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new case after the Egyptian case ended.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that ארץ כנען belongs to all of אברהם's descendants
steps.raayaSupportSource: בראשית 25:12 and 25:19, which call both ישמעאל and יצחק 'son of אברהם'

steps.title: גביהא asks permission to argue again
steps.stepSummary: גביהא בן פסיסא again asks the חכמים for permission to argue, using the same win-win reasoning. They agree, and he goes.
steps.simpleTranslation: גביהא בן פסיסא said to the חכמים: Give me permission to go argue with them before אלכסנדרוס. If they beat me, say: You beat a simple man among us. If I beat them, say: The תורה of משה our teacher beat you. They gave him permission, and he went and argued with them.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. גביהא gets permission so he can answer the new claim in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It is the same pattern as step 23. If גביהא loses, the Jews lose nothing important. If he wins, the victory belongs to the תורה.

keyTerms.meaning: An ordinary, simple person (not a scholar)

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶן גְּבִיהָא בֶּן פְּסִיסָא לַחֲכָמִים:
phrases.english: Geviha ben Pesisa said to the Sages:
Give me permission
and I will go and argue with them
before Alexander of Macedon.
If they defeat me, say:
You have defeated a simple man among us,
and if I defeat them,

phrases.aramaic: אִמְרוּ לָהֶם: תּוֹרַת מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ נִצְּחַתְכֶם.
phrases.english: say to them: The Torah of Moses our teacher defeated you.
They gave him permission,
he went and argued with them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהֶן גְּבִיהָא בֶּן פְּסִיסָא לַחֲכָמִים: תְּנוּ לִי רְשׁוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets up גביהא's reply to the claim in step 27.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: גביהא receives permission to represent the Jews, on the terms that a loss is his own and a win belongs to the תורה.

steps.title: גביהא asks for the source of their proof
steps.stepSummary: גביהא asks where their proof comes from, and they answer: from the תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Where do you bring your proof from? They said to him: From the תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: גביהא first pins down the source of their argument. Their answer sets up his reply in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once they admit their proof is from the תורה, they must accept the rest of the תורה as well. That gives גביהא the ground he needs to answer them.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶם: מֵהֵיכָן אַתֶּם מְבִיאִין רְאָיָיה?
phrases.english: He said to them: From where are you bringing proof?
They said to him: From the Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהֶם: מֵהֵיכָן אַתֶּם מְבִיאִין רְאָיָיה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: גביהא opens his argument, the same way he did in step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They answer that their source is the תורה.

steps.title: אברהם gave everything to יצחק and sent the others away
steps.stepSummary: גביהא quotes the פסוק that אברהם gave all he had to יצחק and gave only gifts to the concubines' sons. A father who divides his estate in his lifetime and sends one son away leaves that son no claim.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: I too will bring proof only from the תורה: 'אברהם gave all that he had to יצחק. And to the sons of the concubines אברהם gave gifts.' If a father gave written gifts of his property to his sons in his lifetime and sent one away from the other, does one have any claim on the other?
steps.whatsHappening: גביהא answers them using the same תורה they quoted. He shows that אברהם himself already settled who gets what.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their claim was based on inheritance after a father dies. גביהא shows that אברהם divided his property while he was still alive: everything went to יצחק and gifts went to the others. Once a father divides his estate himself, the sons who were sent away have nothing more to claim.
steps.whatToRemember: An inheritance claim fails when the father already divided the property himself while alive. אברהם gave the land to יצחק.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think גביהא denies that ישמעאל and קטורה's sons are children of אברהם. He agrees they are. He argues that אברהם chose to give everything to יצחק.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶן: אַף אֲנִי לֹא אָבִיא רְאָיָיה
phrases.english: He said to them: I too will not bring proof
except from the Torah,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״וַיִּתֵּן אַבְרָהָם אֶת כׇּל אֲשֶׁר לוֹ לְיִצְחָק.
phrases.english: as it is said: "And Abraham gave all that he had to Isaac.
And to the sons of the concubines that Abraham had,
Abraham gave gifts."
A father who gave documents of gift to his sons during his lifetime
and sent one away from the other,

phrases.aramaic: כְּלוּם יֵשׁ לָזֶה עַל זֶה כְּלוּם?
phrases.english: does this one have any claim at all against that one?
phrases.notes: He means the son who was sent away has no claim on the son who got the property.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַף אֲנִי לֹא אָבִיא רְאָיָיה אֶלָּא מִן הַתּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses their own source, the תורה, to defeat their claim from step 27.
steps.raayaObject: That the land belongs to יצחק alone and the other sons have no claim
steps.raayaSupportSource: בראשית 25:5–6, together with the rule that a father who divides his estate in his lifetime leaves no claim to a son he sent away
steps.whyThisMatters: It turns their inheritance argument around. The same chapter of the תורה that they quoted shows that אברהם gave the land to יצחק.

steps.title: What were the gifts?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the 'gifts' were that אברהם gave the concubines' sons.
steps.simpleTranslation: What were the gifts?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא steps aside from the story to ask about a word in the פסוק. This is a setup for the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since 'all that he had' went to יצחק, it is unclear what was left to give as 'gifts.' The גמרא wants to know what these gifts were.

phrases.english: What were the gifts?
phrases.notes: This goes back to the word מתנות in the פסוק quoted in the step before.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי מַתָּנוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about a word in the פסוק that גביהא quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the 'gifts' to the concubines' sons were

steps.title: רבי ירמיה בר אבא: a name of impurity
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה בר אבא explains that the gifts were a 'שם טומאה', a name of impure power, which אברהם handed over to them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה בר אבא said: This teaches that he handed over to them a name of impurity.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question. The 'gifts' were not property but a name of impure, supernatural power.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This fits with 'all that he had' going to יצחק. The other sons did not get any of the land or the estate; they got a different kind of 'gift' altogether.

keyTerms.meaning: A name of impurity, a name of impure power used for witchcraft

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba said:
This teaches that he handed over to them a name of impurity.
phrases.notes: "He" is אברהם, and "them" are the sons of the concubines.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא: מְלַמֵּד שֶׁמָּסַר לָהֶם שֵׁם טוּמְאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 31.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The gifts were a 'שם טומאה', a name of impure power, not property.

steps.title: אנטונינוס argues that body and soul can each blame the other
steps.stepSummary: אנטונינוס tells רבי that the body and soul can escape judgment, because each one can claim the other did the sinning.
steps.simpleTranslation: אנטונינוס said to רבי: The body and the soul can get themselves out of judgment. How? The body says: The soul sinned, because since the day it left me I lie in the grave like a silent stone. The soul says: The body sinned, because since the day I left it I fly in the air like a bird.
steps.whatsHappening: A new story begins. אנטונינוס challenges the idea that a person can be punished after death, since the body and the soul can each blame the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The argument is that neither one sins when it is alone. The body without the soul is lifeless like a stone, and the soul without the body floats harmlessly like a bird. So each side says, 'The sin must have come from the other one,' and it seems no one can be held responsible.

keyTerms.meaning: A Roman emperor who was friendly with רבי and often discussed questions with him
To free themselves from judgment, meaning to escape punishment

phrases.english: Antoninos said to Rabbi:
phrases.notes: "רבי" here is רבי יהודה הנשיא, who wrote down the משנה.

phrases.english: The body and the soul are able
to exempt themselves from judgment.
How so?
The body says: The soul sinned,
for from the day it departed from me
I lie cast like a silent stone in the grave.
And the soul says: The body sinned,
for from the day I departed from it
I fly in the air like a bird.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַנְטוֹנִינוּס לְרַבִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story. It follows the earlier stories of debates with non-Jewish leaders.
steps.kashyaTarget: The belief that a person is punished after death for their sins
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Each part acts innocently on its own: the body is like a still stone and the soul is like a free bird. So each can blame the other, and neither can be judged.

steps.title: רבי begins answering with a parable of a king's orchard
steps.stepSummary: רבי starts to answer אנטונינוס with a parable about a human king who owned a beautiful orchard.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I will give you a parable. What is this like? It is like a human king who had a beautiful orchard, and in it there were...
steps.whatsHappening: רבי begins his answer by setting up a parable. The story is cut off here and continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of arguing directly, רבי uses a story to show what is wrong with the argument. Right now we only hear the setting: a king and his lovely orchard. The point of the story comes later.

keyTerms.meaning: A parable, a story used to explain an idea
What is this like? A phrase that opens a parable
A king of flesh and blood, meaning a human king

phrases.english: He said to him: I will tell you a parable.
To what is the matter comparable?
To a king of flesh and blood
who had a beautiful orchard,
and there were in it
phrases.notes: The sentence stops in the middle. It continues right away on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אֶמְשׁוֹל לְךָ מָשָׁל. לְמָה הַדָּבָר דּוֹמֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבי begins to answer the argument of אנטונינוס from step 33.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: So far only the opening of the parable: a human king with a beautiful orchard. The full answer comes on the next amud.
